title: Lost in Tokyo
level: художественный текст (от первого лица) B2+–C1, задания B1+–B2
text: The announcement that the train was terminating at the next station came in a language I could not understand, and by the time I realised what was happening, the doors had closed behind me. I was standing in a vast underground station in Tokyo with a suitcase, a dying phone and an address written on a scrap of paper. My aunt, who was supposed to meet me, had given me one piece of advice before I left: 'Whatever happens, stay calm.' I was already failing. A cold draught blew through the corridors, carrying the smell of food from somewhere I could not locate.

Hundreds of people streamed past, each one apparently certain of the destination. The signs offered a bewildering mixture of symbols, numbers and coloured lines, and my head was spinning. I tried asking a young man in a suit, but he apologised quickly in English, bowed and hurried off. A second attempt, with a woman carrying shopping bags, ended in a polite shake of the head. I began to feel that the whole city was gently, courteously refusing to help me. Somewhere above, a cheerful voice announced something, and everyone smiled except me.

It was an elderly lady with a small umbrella who finally stopped. She studied my piece of paper for a long time, then looked at me and said something I did not follow. When I shrugged helplessly, she smiled, took my arm and set off at a surprising speed, leading me through corridors, up an escalator and across a street where the traffic lights chirped like birds. I trotted behind her, dragging my suitcase, with no idea whether I was being rescued or merely taken for a walk. She never stopped talking, and although I understood perhaps one word in twenty, her tone was so reassuring that I stopped feeling afraid.

Twenty minutes later we stood in front of a narrow building squeezed between two offices. That it was the right one was a **stroke of luck**, since my aunt was waiting on its steps, looking pale and holding her telephone as if it were a weapon. She had been searching the nearest stations for almost an hour. I had expected to feel only relief, but to my surprise I felt slightly ashamed, as if I had broken a promise. A small crowd of commuters had stopped to watch the reunion, and a boy of about six waved at me solemnly, as if I had returned from a long voyage.

My aunt, on seeing me, went from relief to anger and back to relief within a few seconds. She thanked the old lady with a deep bow, and the old lady, to my surprise, took a small paper bag from her pocket and pressed it into my hand. Inside were three wrapped sweets. I wanted to say something clever and grateful, but I was lost for words, and in the end I simply bowed, rather badly.

That evening, in my aunt's small kitchen, I ate noodles and told the story three times, each time making myself a little braver. Only later, when I was falling asleep, did I realise that what I remembered best was neither the panic nor the noise but the sweet taste in the dark and the feeling of someone's hand on my arm. I had come to Tokyo to see a great city. I think I had actually come to be reminded that strangers can be kind. I still keep one of the sweet wrappers between the pages of my notebook.

questions.q: How did the narrator feel at the beginning of the story?
Who does 'She' in 'She thanked the old lady with a deep bow' refer to?
'A stroke of luck' in paragraph 4 means …
Why did the first people the narrator spoke to not help her?
options: They were too angry to listen.
They could not give her useful answers.

questions.q: How did the narrator feel as she followed the old lady?
Which of these is NOT mentioned in the text?
options: The old lady asked for payment.
The narrator's phone was not working.
The aunt was relieved to see her.
The old lady gave the narrator a present.

questions.q: What did the narrator realise at the end?
options: Kindness from strangers mattered most to her.
She should have learnt the language.

discuss: Have you ever been lost in an unfamiliar place? What happened?
The author trusted strangers. When is it right to ask a stranger for help?
What would you most like to see in Japan?
